hook.text: Traditional cities shed rain like a shell. Sponge cities absorb it like, well, a sponge.

buildup.text: Permeable pavement, rain gardens, and bioswales let water soak into the ground instead of flooding streets.

discovery.text: China launched its Sponge City initiative in 2015, redesigning 30 pilot cities to absorb stormwater.

twist.text: Sponge infrastructure costs less than concrete drainage — and it recharges groundwater naturally.

climax.text: As extreme rainfall intensifies with climate change, every city needs sponge-like qualities.

punchline.text: A city that drinks its own rain doesn't drown in it.

quiz.question: What is a sponge city designed to do?
options: Absorb stormwater naturally instead of channeling it away
Collect rainwater in rooftop tanks only

details.summary: Sponge cities use permeable surfaces, rain gardens, bioswales, wetlands, and green roofs to absorb stormwater naturally instead of channeling it through pipes. China has invested heavily in the concept, aiming to absorb 70 percent of rainwater in pilot cities by redesigning urban landscapes.
details.whyItMatters: Conventional drainage systems are overwhelmed by intense rainfall events made worse by climate change. Sponge city design reduces flooding while recharging aquifers and improving water quality.
takeaways: Permeable surfaces absorb rain instead of funneling it into drains
China is piloting sponge city projects in dozens of cities
Green infrastructure reduces flooding and recharges groundwater

faq.question: How do sponge cities manage heavy rainfall?
faq.answer: By replacing impervious surfaces with permeable pavement, adding rain gardens and bioswales, restoring wetlands, and planting extensively. These features slow runoff, filter pollutants, and allow water to soak into the ground rather than overwhelm storm drains.

faq.question: Are sponge cities effective during extreme floods?
faq.answer: Sponge city features handle moderate rainfall well but can be overwhelmed during extreme events. They work best as part of a layered approach that also includes flood reservoirs, early warning systems, and conventional drainage as backup during severe storms.
